title: Error Boundaries
description: Learn how to catch JavaScript errors in component trees with error boundaries.

data.text: Error boundaries are React components that catch JavaScript errors anywhere in their child component tree, log those errors, and display a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole app.
The Problem: Uncaught Errors Break the UI
Before error boundaries, a single uncaught error in one component would unmount the entire React tree. The user would see a blank screen with no way to recover without refreshing.

data.title: Error Without Boundary
data.content: An error in one component crashes everything

data.text: Error boundaries are class components that define either or both of these lifecycle methods: getDerivedStateFromError() and componentDidCatch().

terms.definition: A class component that catches errors in its children and renders a fallback UI.
A static lifecycle method that updates state when an error is caught, triggering a fallback render.
A lifecycle method for side effects like logging the error to an external service.
The alternate UI shown when an error is caught, e.g. a friendly error message and retry button.

data.title: ErrorBoundary Class Component

data.text: Wrap any part of your app that might throw in an ErrorBoundary. You can nest boundaries to isolate failures to specific sections.

data.title: Wrapping Risky Components
What Error Boundaries Catch
items: Rendering errors (inside render or lifecycle methods)
Errors in constructors of the whole tree
Errors in the initial mount and updates

data.title: What They Do NOT Catch
items: Errors thrown in the boundary itself

data.title: Event Handlers Need Try/Catch
data.text: Error boundaries do not catch errors inside event handlers. Wrap handler logic in try/catch and set error state manually.

data.caption: How an error boundary isolates a failing component from the rest of the app.
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[App Tree] --> B[ErrorBoundary]
    B -->|no error| C[Normal Child UI]
    B -->|error caught| D[Fallback UI]
    E[Sibling Component] --> F[Still Visible]

data.title: Exercise: Add an Error Boundary
data.description: Wrap a data-heavy component with an error boundary and display a friendly fallback.
steps: Create an ErrorBoundary class component with getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch.
Wrap a UserProfile component that fetches and renders user data.
Throw an error inside UserProfile if the data is malformed.
Verify that the fallback UI appears and the rest of the app stays visible.
data.expectedOutcome: A page where a broken component shows a fallback without taking down the whole app.

items.question: Why are error boundaries class components?
items.answer: Error boundaries require lifecycle methods (getDerivedStateFromError, componentDidCatch) that are not yet available in hooks. React may add a useErrorBoundary hook in the future.

items.question: Can I share state between the boundary and its children?
items.answer: Not directly. The boundary controls the fallback UI. If children need to recover, expose a reset function via context or lift the state up.

items.question: Should every component have its own boundary?
items.answer: No. Place boundaries strategically around sections that might fail independently, such as a dashboard, a widget, or a third-party embed.

items.question: Do error boundaries catch errors in the boundary itself?
items.answer: No. If the boundary's render or lifecycle throws, the nearest boundary above it catches it. If there is no boundary above it, the app unmounts.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Error boundaries catch rendering errors in the component tree.
They are class components using getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch.
Wrap risky sections to isolate failures and keep the rest of the app alive.
They do not catch event handlers, async code, or SSR errors.
data.takeaway: Error boundaries make your app resilient. Combined with proper logging, they turn crashes into recoverable moments.
